title: State Harmonization Model for Multi-Region Control Plane
content:
Purpose
This note captures a pragmatic, implementable model for control-plane data harmonization across regions and clusters, with concrete CRUD API semantics and routing-policy evaluation constraints. The intent is to move beyond ad-hoc fanout designs and provide clear invariants for:
 - eventual convergence of resource state across regions
 - deterministic routing decisions under stale reads
 - safe, idempotent CRUD operations for platform consumers and downstream controllers

High-level goals and tradeoffs
1) Availability-first but bounded-staleness: the control plane must accept writes in the local region for latency/availability while providing guarantees that replicas converge within an operational bound (e.g., 30s–5m depending on resource criticality).
2) Strong intent semantics for user-driven changes: user-visible mutations must be expressed as desired-state changes (declarative) with versioned revisions, not ad-hoc imperative edits that are hard to reconcile.
3) Deterministic routing: routing policy evaluation must be reproducible from resource metadata + region-local snapshot so that fallback/preview behavior is predictable.

Concepts and primitives
- Resource record: canonical user-facing object stored in the control plane. Core fields (example):
  - id: global-uuid
  - kind: resource kind (model, endpoint, route, pool)
  - owner: team/service id
  - tenancy: shared|dedicated|private
  - desired_state: JSON blob (declarative config)
  - observed_state: compact status summary
  - region_bindings: list of bindings {region -> cluster_selector, affinity_policy}
  - revision: monotonic integer (logical)
  - etag: opaque fingerprint (sha256 of desired_state+revision)
  - tombstone: boolean (soft delete)
  - last_updated_at: ISO8601

- Revision vs. ETag semantics: revision increments on any accepted write. ETag is computed after the write and used for conditional updates. Clients should use If-Match semantics for strong optimistic concurrency.

- Conflict domain: conflicts only occur per-resource id. Cross-resource invariants (e.g., two routes mapping to the same external port) are validated by the coordinator and reconciled via reject-on-violation semantics at write time.

Replication model and anti-entropy
- Leaderless, multi-master write acceptance: any region can accept a write for a resource, returning a provisional revision and a globally unique operation id (op_id).
- Anti-entropy stream: regions exchange ordered operation logs (oplogs) per resource id. Oplogs carry: op_id, origin_region, base_revision, delta_patch (json-patch), new_revision, timestamp, signature. Oplog application is idempotent and driven by base_revision checks.
- Reconciliation rules: when receiving an oplog whose base_revision != current local revision, the receiver attempts a three-way merge (local_latest, base_snapshot, incoming_patch). Merge fallbacks: apply if patch is commutative, else mark resource as conflicted and create a reconciliation job for human/operator or automated resolution policy.
- Conflict resolution policies:
  - deterministic-last-writer-fast-path: if timestamps differ by > configurable skew and no overlapping fields touched, accept latest.
  - field-level arithmetic merges for counters/quotas.
  - prefer origin-region writes for region-scoped fields (region_binding, cluster_affinity) when conflicting with non-affinity edits.
  - explicit lock/lease mechanism for high-risk edits (see API section).

Garbage collection and tombstone handling
- Soft delete via tombstone + retention window (e.g., 7 days). During retention, tombstoned records remain in oplogs for reconciliation. After retention, tombstones are compacted from logs.
- A separate GC epoch process ensures cross-region removal only after consensus of tombstone visibility and dependent resource checks (no active routes/policies reference it).

Routing policy evaluation under staleness
- Routing policy must be expressible from resource metadata and small, region-local runtime inputs (capacity, latency buckets).
- Evaluation snapshot: each runtime uses the last known control-plane revision for the resource plus local metrics. We define a monotonically increasing routing_epoch attached to routing-config updates; nodes must not accept route decisions from an epoch older than a configurable TTL.
- Fallback rules: if route target cluster is unknown or reported offline, evaluation should:
  1) consult preferred-region fallback list embedded in resource record;
  2) fall back to nearest-available compatible model variant;
  3) route to a degraded-capacity tier if no full-capacity cluster is available.

API design: CRUD semantics and examples
Principles: idempotency, conditional updates, and small coarse-grained operations to reduce merge complexity. Use REST/JSON over HTTPS with ETag and optimistic concurrency.

- Create (POST /v1/resources)
  - Body: resource payload without id (server generates uuid).
  - Response: 201 Created with body {id, revision, etag, op_id}.
  - Create is idempotent if client provides client_generated_id header (idempotency-key).

- Read (GET /v1/resources/{id})
  - Returns full record + revision + etag + last_applied_op_id.
  - Support ?projection=desired_state,observed_state or minimal.

- Update (PUT /v1/resources/{id})
  - Full replace authorized. Client must supply If-Match: "etag" header to guarantee revision. Server rejects with 412 if mismatch.
  - On success returns new revision and etag.

- Patch (PATCH /v1/resources/{id})
  - Accepts json-patch or strategic-merge; server validates base_etag or If-Match. PATCH is preferred for minor deltas to improve merge success during oplog apply.

- Delete (DELETE /v1/resources/{id})
  - Soft-delete sets tombstone true and increments revision. Supports If-Match optional. Immediate hard-delete only via admin endpoint and behind GC checks.

- Acquire lease (POST /v1/resources/{id}:acquire-lease)
  - For high-conflict edits: clients request a short lease (30s–5m) to serialize edits. Response includes lease_id and expiry. Leases accepted region-locally but propagated in oplog metadata so other regions delay conflicting merges.

Operational invariants and monitoring
- Metric set: oplog-lag (per-region percentile), reconciliation-queue-depth, conflicted-resources-count, tombstone-retention-age, stale-read-rate (requests served from revision older than N seconds).
- SLO guidance: 99th-percentile oplog-lag < 10s for non-critical resources; < 60s for low-priority annotations.

Scenarios and examples
1) Fast local update with cross-region conflict: dev in EU edits route affinity to prefer eu-west. US region also edits traffic-split minutes later. Anti-entropy produces two oplogs; reconciler applies field-level merge (traffic weights sum-normalized) or marks as conflict if both edited identical weight fields.
2) Region outage: if eu-west control-plane unavailable, local eu runtime continues to read last-known revision and route according to fallback list. When control-plane returns, oplog replay reconciles any local edge-only changes using three-way merge.

Next steps and open questions
- Evaluate replacing oplog three-way merges with lightweight CRDTs for selected resource kinds (routes, quotas).
- Define clear operator workflows for manual reconcile when automated policies mark resource conflicted.
- Implementation spike: small prototype that publishes oplogs to Kafka topic per-resource-id and a reconciler consumer that demonstrates three-way merge heuristics.

Appendix: small API example (simplified)
POST /v1/resources
Body:
{
  "kind": "route",
  "owner": "payments-service",
  "desired_state": {"match":"/v1/pay","weight": {"eu": 80, "us": 20}},
  "region_bindings": [{"region":"eu-west","cluster_selector":"gpu-prod-*","affinity":"prefer"}]
}
Response:
{
  "id": "rsc_14f3a...",
  "revision": 1,
  "etag": "sha256:abcd...",
  "op_id": "op_eu_20260122_0007"
}

This doc is intentionally prescriptive: it balances practical implementability with conservative guarantees that enable low-latency writes and predictable routing. Feedback welcome — especially on tradeoffs for leases vs CRDTs and concrete numbering for oplog TTLs and retention windows.
